The true kettle drum may have begun with an animal hide stretched over a clay jar, and wood or turtle shell were also used early on. Mesopotamian tablets record a bronze drum of the Achaemenid empire, the lilissu, faced with cowhide and used in religious ritual. Kettle drums served for a long time as war drums, appearing on Parthian battlefields, and were later developed by Middle Eastern cultures such as the Sasanian and Byzantine empires into the naqareh, reaching Europe and India and becoming the naker and the nagara. The English name appears in a text of 1542 from Thomas Seymour to Henry VIII, because the king ordered several sets from Vienna for war.

Other contexts include the religious ritual of the Mesopotamian bronze drum lilissu or lilis, and use on the Parthian cavalry battlefield for coordination and intimidation; the Sasanian empire paired it with a horn or trumpet. Afterwards this kind of drum developed into forms such as the naqareh, the naker and the nagara in the Middle East, Byzantium, Europe and India, and the cultures of South Asia and the Middle East have their own kettle-drum types.

A kettle drum is a membranophone percussion instrument with an animal hide stretched over a large hemispherical bowl, sounding when struck. The bowl is traditionally of copper or bronze, and clay and wood are also found; the head is most often calfskin, and can be tuned by rope tension or by a hoop-and-bolt system. The most common in Western music is the timpani, whose name is almost synonymous with the kettle drum; most cultures of the Middle East and South Asia have their own types. Its Hornbostel–Sachs number is 211.1. Historically the kettle drum has been used to coordinate on the battlefield, in cavalry units and in religious ritual, as for example the bronze drums of Mesopotamia used in sacrifice, while the Parthian empire used it to direct troops in battle.
鍋鼓的碗形鼓身傳統上以銅或青銅製成，亦見陶、木等材質；早期可能以陶罐蒙皮，或曾用: The bowl-shaped body of a kettle drum is traditionally of copper or bronze, and pottery and wood are also found; early ones may have been a clay jar with a skin over it, or wood or turtle shell may at some time have been used. The head is usually animal skin, most often calfskin, and after synthetic heads appeared in the twentieth century many kettle drums still use animal skin. Fixing and tuning methods include traditional rope tension and the more modern hoop and bolts, while nailing or gluing is less common.

Because the bowl reflects the main note of the head, most kettle drums, such as the timpani and the tabla, produce a definite pitch when struck. Tuning can be by rope tension or by a hoop-and-bolt system; the source gives neither the range nor how the volume is controlled. Compared with other types in the family, the shared feature of kettle drums is a head stretched over a hemispherical bowl, and in the West the timpani are the most common.
